---
title: "Week 7 — Probability, Sampling, and Sampling Distributions"
---

### Why This Week Matters

Quantitative anthropologists almost never observe an entire population.
Archaeologists cannot excavate every square meter, date every surviving
sample, or recover everything that once existed. Week 7 asks how we can
reason responsibly from **partial observations**.

Sampling creates uncertainty in two different ways. Even a well-designed
random sample varies by chance from one sample to another: **sampling
variability**. A sampling frame or selection process can also
systematically overrepresent some parts of a population and
underrepresent others: **sampling bias**. A larger sample can reduce the
first problem without necessarily correcting the second.

Assignment 4 applies these ideas to archaeological radiocarbon
determinations from the p3k14c project.

## What You Should Understand

By the end of Week 7, you should be able to:

1.  explain probability as a long-run relative frequency;
2.  distinguish **population/sample** and **parameter/statistic**;
3.  explain a **sampling frame** and why it matters;
4.  distinguish probability from nonprobability sampling;
5.  explain **sampling with versus without replacement**;
6.  explain **sampling variability** and a **sampling distribution**;
7.  distinguish standard deviation from **standard error** and explain
    the effect of sample size;
8.  state the Central Limit Theorem at an introductory level and avoid
    common misconceptions;
9.  distinguish **sampling variability from sampling bias**;
10. explain why a large sample can be precise but unrepresentative; and
11. apply these ideas to radiocarbon databases and p3k14c.

# 1. Probability as Long-Run Frequency

Probability gives us a language for uncertainty. In the frequentist
interpretation used here, probability is understood through repeated
trials. A fair coin has probability 0.5 of landing heads, but ten flips
need not contain exactly five heads. Short runs fluctuate.

As the number of repeated trials becomes very large, the observed
proportion tends to stabilize near the underlying probability.

> **Random does not mean patternless. Short runs can fluctuate
> substantially even when the long-run probability is stable.**

This prepares us for sampling: a random sample can differ noticeably
from its population simply by chance.

# 2. Population, Sample, Parameter, and Statistic

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Population world                    Sample world
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  **Population** --- complete target  **Sample** --- observed subset
  universe                            

  **Parameter** --- numerical         **Statistic** --- numerical
  property of the population          property calculated from a sample

  Population mean: (`\mu`{=tex})      Sample mean: (`\bar`{=tex}{x})

  Population SD: (`\sigma`{=tex})     Sample SD: (s)

  Population proportion: (P)          Sample proportion: (p)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

A statistic estimates a parameter, but it is not the parameter itself.
Different random samples from the same population usually produce
somewhat different statistics.

# 3. The Sampling Frame

The **target population** is what we want to make claims about. The
**sampling frame** is the operational set of cases from which
observations can actually be selected: a list, database, register, site
inventory, survey grid, or other accessible collection.

> **A sample directly represents the frame from which it was selected,
> not automatically every population we would like it to represent.**

If part of the target population is absent from the frame, random
selection cannot recover what is missing.

**Target population → Sampling frame → Sample → Statistic**

# 4. Probability and Nonprobability Sampling

## Probability sampling

Units have known, non-zero probabilities of selection. Designs
introduced in the lecture include simple random, systematic, stratified,
and cluster/PPS sampling. Probability sampling matters because the
selection process is explicitly modeled and, under appropriate
conditions, sampling uncertainty can be quantified.

## Nonprobability sampling

Purposive, quota, theoretical, snowball/RDS, and convenience sampling
can be appropriate for particular research goals, especially qualitative
depth, pilot research, expert knowledge, and hard-to-reach populations.

The limitation is inferential: if selection probabilities are unknown,
ordinary probability-sampling logic cannot simply be used to estimate
sampling error for population parameters.

# 5. Sampling With and Without Replacement

**Without replacement:** once selected, a case cannot be selected again
in the same sample.

**With replacement:** after selection, the case returns to the available
pool and can be selected again.

In R:

``` r
sample(x, size = 25, replace = TRUE)
```

Assignment 4 uses sampling with replacement to simulate repeated random
sampling from a fixed teaching population. This does not mean
archaeologists literally excavate the same object repeatedly. It creates
a repeated-sampling model in which each draw comes from the same
reference distribution.

# 6. Sampling Variability

Draw several independent random samples of the same size and calculate a
mean for each:

\[
`\bar`{=tex}{x}\_1, `\bar`{=tex}{x}\_2, `\bar`{=tex}{x}\_3, `\bar`{=tex}{x}\_4, `\bar`{=tex}{x}\_5
\]

They will usually differ. This is **sampling variability**: a statistic
changes from one random sample to another because different observations
happen to be selected.

Cumming calls this the **"dance of the means."** Sampling variability is
not evidence that random sampling failed; it is an unavoidable
consequence of observing only part of a variable population.

# 7. Sampling Distributions

Imagine repeating the sampling process many times. For each repetition:

1.  draw a random sample of size (n);
2.  calculate its mean;
3.  save that mean; and
4.  repeat.

The collection of sample means forms the **sampling distribution of the
sample mean**.

> **A data distribution describes individual observations. A sampling
> distribution describes a statistic across repeated samples.**

In Assignment 4, individual conventional radiocarbon ages form the
distribution of `age`; 1,000 means from 1,000 repeated samples form an
empirical sampling distribution of the mean.

# 8. Sample Size and Standard Error

Larger random samples tend to produce more stable estimates:

**small (n) → more variable sample means → wider sampling distribution**

**large (n) → less variable sample means → narrower sampling
distribution**

The **standard error (SE)** describes the spread of a sampling
distribution. For a sample mean:

\[ SE\_{`\bar`{=tex}{x}}=`\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}`{=tex} \]

When (`\sigma`{=tex}) is unknown, (s/`\sqrt{n}`{=tex}) is commonly used
as an estimate.

Because SE changes with the square root of (n), doubling sample size
does not halve SE. Approximately **four times the sample size is
required to halve the standard error**.

## Standard deviation versus standard error

**SD** describes variability among individual observations.

**SE** describes variability of a statistic across repeated samples.

# 9. The Central Limit Theorem

At an introductory level, the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) tells us that,
under appropriate conditions, the sampling distribution of a mean tends
toward a normal distribution as sample size increases.

The important object is the **sampling distribution**, not the raw
observations.

The CLT does **not** mean that raw data become normal when (n) is large,
that every population must be normal, or that (n `\ge 30`{=tex})
guarantees normality in every situation. The lecture emphasizes
independence and finite variance, and convergence also depends on
features such as skewness and tail behavior.

For ANTH418, the main importance of the CLT is conceptual: it helps
explain why sampling distributions can become predictable enough to
support statistical inference.

# 10. Sampling Variability Is Not Sampling Bias

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Sampling variability                Sampling bias
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Random fluctuation                  Systematic distortion

  Occurs even with good random        Arises from the frame or selection
  sampling                            process

  Different samples give different    Some parts are systematically over-
  statistics                          or underrepresented

  Generally decreases as (n)          Does not necessarily disappear as
  increases                           (n) increases

  Reflected in SE                     Not repaired simply by obtaining a
                                      smaller SE
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

> **A very large biased sample can provide a highly precise estimate of
> the wrong target quantity.**

A small SE means repeated samples from the **same sampling process**
would give similar estimates. It does not prove that the process
represents the intended target population.

# 11. Sample Size versus Sample Quality

The Literary Digest example in the lecture demonstrates why a huge
sample can perform badly when its sampling frame systematically
underrepresents important groups.

Increasing (n) helps with random sampling variability. It does not
automatically correct coverage bias, selection bias, nonresponse bias,
geographic imbalance, or research-history bias.

Before asking "How large is the sample?", also ask:

> **How did these observations become eligible to enter the sample?**

# 12. Archaeological Application: Dates-as-Data

Radiocarbon databases are large but strongly filtered collections:

**Past human activity → datable material → preservation → archaeological
discovery → sample selection → laboratory dating → database inclusion →
observed radiocarbon distribution**

Filters include preservation, decay and erosion as well as excavation
history, research interests, funding, access, choices about what to
date, and database compilation.

> **A radiocarbon database is not a census of past human activity.**

A raw distribution of dates can reflect both prehistoric processes and
modern research behavior.

# 13. Bird et al. (2022) and p3k14c

Bird et al. assembled and standardized a very large global database of
archaeological radiocarbon dates and evaluated dimensions of data
quality and sampling coverage.

For Week 7, the crucial lesson is not simply that p3k14c is large. It is
that **large databases can remain unevenly sampled**.

The lecture highlights geographic imbalance and Bird et al.'s comparison
of radiocarbon-date density with archaeological-site density. Some
regions have disproportionately many dates relative to sites; others
have relatively few.

This demonstrates the same statistical principle:

> **Large (n) does not guarantee representativeness.**

# 14. Reading Guide

## Bernard --- Probability Sampling

Focus on target populations, sampling frames, random selection,
representativeness, sampling bias, and the scope of legitimate
generalization. The key lesson is that **sampling design determines the
scope of inference**.

## Cumming --- The Normal Distribution and Sampling

Focus on population parameters versus sample statistics, the "dance of
the means," the "mean heap," sampling distributions, standard error, the
relationship between (n) and SE, and the CLT.

The visual intuition is especially important: repeated sample means
"dance," but larger samples produce a narrower dance.

## Bird et al. --- p3k14c

Read the database as a **sampling problem**, not simply a source of
dates. Ask where the dates came from, how they were assembled and
standardized, whether geographic coverage is even, how sampling
intensity is evaluated, and how research history may affect the observed
distribution.

## Thulin --- Recommended Computational Support

Use Thulin for simulation in R: repeated simulation, random sampling,
`sample()`, sampling with replacement, `set.seed()`, reproducibility,
and the effect of changing sample size. Later inferential procedures in
the chapter are not required for Assignment 4.

# 15. Assignment 4 Connection

The Southern California teaching file contains **984 radiocarbon
determinations** and is treated as a known **reference population** for
the exercise.

### Experiment 1: Change sample size

Repeated random samples at different (n) values demonstrate:

**larger (n) → less sampling variability → smaller SE → greater
precision**

### Experiment 2: Change the sampling frame

The exercise then restricts the frame geographically. Sampling remains
random **within that restricted frame**, but increasing (n) makes
estimates increasingly stable around the restricted-frame mean. It does
not force them toward the mean of the full teaching population.

Therefore:

**larger (n) can reduce variability without eliminating bias**

This is the central lesson of Assignment 4.

# 16. Common Misunderstandings

-   **"A random sample should look exactly like the population."**
    No. Random samples fluctuate.
-   **"A statistic is the true population value."** No. A statistic
    estimates a parameter.
-   **"A sampling distribution is the histogram of observations in my
    sample."** No. It is a distribution of a statistic across repeated
    samples.
-   **"SD and SE are the same."** No. SD describes observations; SE
    describes sampling variability of a statistic.
-   **"Doubling (n) halves SE."** No. Roughly four times (n) is needed.
-   **"The CLT says large datasets become normal."** No. It concerns
    sampling distributions of statistics under appropriate conditions.
-   **"(n=30) is always enough."** No. There is no universal guarantee.
-   **"A huge sample must be representative."** No. Large biased samples
    can be very precise.
-   **"Random sampling fixes a bad frame."** No. Random selection only
    operates on cases available in the frame.
-   **"A large radiocarbon database directly represents prehistoric
    population."** Not automatically; preservation and research
    processes filter it.

14. Why can a very large sample be precise but unrepresentative?
15. Why can random sampling fail to represent a target population when
    the sampling frame is incomplete?
16. Why should p3k14c not be treated simply as a census of past human
    activity?
17. In Assignment 4, why does increasing sample size within the
    restricted frame reduce variability without necessarily removing
    bias?

# 18. Core Takeaway

Week 7 can be summarized as a chain:

**Population → Sampling frame → Sample → Statistic → Repeated samples →
Sampling distribution → Standard error → Inference**

But statistical precision is only one part of defensible inference.

> **Larger random samples generally reduce sampling variability and
> increase precision, but increasing sample size does not correct a
> systematically biased sampling frame.**

In archaeology, this matters especially because every observed dataset
has already been filtered by preservation, recovery, research history,
selection, and recording practices.
